_: Эпизод Forgotten Fortunes, конвертирован из присланного манифеста forgotten-fortunes-ep03.json под этот конвейер. Текст, промпты, заголовки, описание, теги и политика источников взяты оттуда без правок по смыслу. Изменено только то, что не собралось бы: см. поле _расхождения.
_расхождения: Присланный render-episode.yml НЕ используется. Он строит слайдшоу через zoompan — замерено 31 секунда процессорного времени на секунду видео, на 23 минуты это больше 12 часов при лимите GitHub Actions в 6. Здесь наезды делаются через scale+crop: 2.6 с на секунду.

Сумма hold_seconds у двадцати картинок = 166 секунд против 23 минут начитки. В присланном workflow -shortest обрезал бы звук до 2:46 молча. Здесь длительность каждого кадра считается от границ предложений в тайм-кодах озвучки, поэтому картинка идёт ровно столько, сколько идёт звук.
Поля motion и hold_seconds у картинок не переносятся: движение камеры и длительность назначает движок стиля от позиции на таймлайне и от пауз в речи. Смысл тот же — медленный наезд, отъезд, панорама.
Теги урезаны с 597 символов до лимита YouTube в 500. Убран тег с именем частного лица (terry herbert...): наводить поиск на живого человека по имени не стоит, событие ищется и без этого.
Главы переписаны под границы сегментов: конвейер вычисляет тайм-коды из реальной озвучки, а в манифесте они были проставлены руками и не совпадали с началами сегментов.
Добавлены footage_queries и archive_queries: в манифесте их нет, он рассчитан на слайдшоу из одной генерации. Здесь 30% времени генерация, остальное реальный сток и архив.
_голос: Голос из секрета ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID. voice_settings перенесены из манифеста как есть.
_цветокор: copper_dusk — самый насыщенный из тёплой семьи, под золото и медь. Архивный archive_silver: у pawn-01 был sepia, повторять нельзя.
script_blocks:
The hammer came down so hard that it broke.

Not chipped. Broke. The head snapped clean off the handle, and the auctioneer, a heavy man in his sixties in a tweed jacket, was left standing in a converted warehouse in a west London suburb, holding a stick.

Four seconds earlier, the number on the board had read forty-three million pounds.

For a vase. Sixteen inches tall. That morning it had been sitting on a shelf between a rocking horse and a grandfather clock.

Three objects. Three completely ordinary people. A couple walking their dog. An unemployed man with a second-hand metal detector. A retired solicitor emptying out a dead relative's bungalow.

Between them, in the space of four years, they pulled close to seventy million dollars out of the dirt, out of a ploughed field, and off a dusty shelf. And every single one of them came within inches of walking straight past it.

Here is the part these stories usually leave out.

The finding is the easy bit. Bending down takes a second. What comes afterwards takes years. Valuation committees. Lawyers. Silence. Aeroplanes to countries you have never been to, chasing money that might not exist.

Two of these three people paid for their fortune with something they never got back. A friendship. A name. A life they were allowed to talk about out loud.

And that number I just gave you... the forty-three million that broke the gavel... was never paid. Not one penny of it.

I will come back to that. What happened instead is stranger than the auction.

Start in California.

Early in two thousand and thirteen, in the dry gold country of Northern California, a husband and wife took the same walk they had taken for years. Same path. Same hillside. Same dog.

They were in their forties, self-employed, and they had lived on that rural property for several years. To this day, almost nobody knows their names. In every news story, in every catalogue, they are called John and Mary. Those are not their real names.

It had rained. The bank beside the path had eroded slightly, and something was poking up out of the mud. A can. Old, rusted, dented. The kind of thing you kick aside a hundred times without a second thought.

She bent down anyway.

The coin dealer who later handled the find repeated what she told him about that moment. Don't be above bending over to check on a rusty can.

It didn't move. It was far heavier than a can that size has any business being. Gold is dense. A tin packed tight with double eagles weighs roughly what a bowling ball weighs.

They carried it back to the house and opened it on the kitchen counter. Inside, stacked on edge, packed so tightly they had to be prised apart, were gold coins.

Then they went back outside with a shovel.

Over the following days they dug up eight cans in total, at different depths, near the roots of an old tree on a path they had walked hundreds of times. Between them, those cans held one thousand four hundred and twenty-seven gold coins, minted between eighteen forty-seven and eighteen ninety-four.

The face value, the number actually stamped into the metal, came to twenty-seven thousand, nine hundred and eighty dollars.

That was not what they were worth.

For months, the couple told nobody. Not friends, not neighbours. They put the coins into an old ice chest, buried the ice chest under a woodpile in their own yard, and went to bed every night about thirty feet away from roughly ten million dollars.

Eventually they drove the coins, in plastic bags, to a numismatic firm in Tiburon called Kagin's. The senior numismatist there, David McCarthy, later described picking the first one out of a bag. An eighteen ninety double eagle, filthy, crusted with rust and clay. He turned it to the light, and through the tiny patch of exposed metal he could see that the coin underneath was essentially perfect.

That is the detail that changes everything. These coins had been buried in cans for well over a century, and most of them had never circulated. They came out of the ground looking like they had come out of the mint.

The breakdown: one thousand three hundred and seventy-three twenty-dollar Liberty double eagles, fifty ten-dollar eagles, and four five-dollar half eagles. Most were struck at the San Francisco mint. More than a dozen of them were graded as the finest examples of their date and mint that anyone has ever certified.

One coin, an eighteen sixty-six San Francisco double eagle without the motto, was valued on its own at close to one million dollars.

The whole hoard was put at ten million dollars and up. The largest buried cache of gold coins ever recovered in the United States.

And then the internet went to work.

Within days there were theories. The gold belonged to Jesse James. The gold belonged to the stagecoach robber Black Bart. Best of all, the gold was stolen, lifted from the San Francisco mint in a famous embezzlement at the turn of the century, which would mean the couple owned nothing at all and would have to hand every coin back.

Newspapers ran it. Serious newspapers. For a few weeks, the biggest treasure find in American history looked like it might evaporate in a courtroom.

It didn't. The dates were wrong. A mint theft would have produced uncirculated coins of one or two recent years, all with the same mint mark. This hoard was mixed, spanning nearly fifty years, and plenty of the coins had clearly been in someone's pocket. The United States Mint issued a plain statement of its own. It had no information linking the Saddle Ridge coins to any theft at any mint facility.

So the couple kept them.

The sale opened at midnight on the twenty-seventh of May, two thousand and fourteen, on Amazon and on the dealer's own website. Not an auction. A shopping cart. Over a million dollars of gold sold in the first couple of hours. In the first twenty-four hours, Amazon moved three hundred and forty-six coins for just under one point four million dollars, and the dealer sold two hundred and twenty-five more for over two point four million.

Buyers came from France, Germany, Japan, Britain, Canada, Brazil, Hong Kong.

The couple paid off their debts. They gave money to local charities. They kept a small handful of coins for themselves and let the rest go.

And here is what they gave up.

They can never be named. Not now, not in twenty years. The moment they are, the property becomes a target, and every stranger with a family story about a great-grandfather in the gold fields has a reason to knock on their door. Several people came forward claiming the gold had belonged to their ancestors. None of them got anywhere.

So the single most extraordinary thing that will ever happen to these two people is a thing they have to pretend never happened. No interviews. No photographs. Just a rusty can in a museum case somewhere, and a name that isn't theirs.

There is one more loss in this story, and it is not theirs.

Somebody buried that gold. Somebody put away one thousand four hundred and twenty-seven coins, in eight separate cans, over what looks like decades. Coin by coin by coin. That person walked away from a fortune and never came back for it. Never told anyone where it was, or told one person who didn't listen.

Nobody knows who they were. Nobody ever will.

In California, the ground gave up a fortune and nobody could prove whose it was.

Five thousand miles away, a man had the opposite problem. Everyone knew exactly what he had found, exactly who it belonged to, and exactly what it was worth, down to the pound.

That was the problem.

The fifth of July, two thousand and nine. Terry Herbert, fifty-five years old, from Burntwood in Staffordshire, England. Unemployed. Living on disability benefit in a council flat.

He had been metal detecting for about eighteen years. Eighteen years of ring pulls, bottle caps, Victorian pennies and horseshoes. His detector was second-hand, picked up at a car boot sale, reportedly for two pounds fifty.

That morning he drove a few minutes down the road to a field near the village of Hammerwich, pronounced hammer-witch, just outside Lichfield. The field belonged to a farmer he knew, Fred Johnson, sixty-eight years old, who had given him permission to search. It had just been ploughed.

Within about half an hour, the detector screamed.

He dug. Gold. Not a coin, not a ring. A piece of ornament, twisted, unmistakably old.

He moved a metre, and it screamed again.

For five days he went back to that field, and for five days the gold kept coming out of the soil. He filled bag after bag. Two hundred and forty-four of them.

He said afterwards that it was like being at home while somebody keeps putting money through your letterbox. He told a newspaper it was more fun than winning the lottery. He also said that when he closed his eyes at night, he was still seeing gold.

To his enormous credit, he stopped. He could have kept digging in silence. Instead he called the local finds liaison officer and handed the field over to archaeologists.

What came out of the ground over the following months rewrote a century of scholarship.

Around four thousand objects. Roughly five kilograms of gold. Another one and a half kilos of silver. Three and a half thousand cut garnets, some of them from as far away as India or Sri Lanka. Seventh century. The kingdom of Mercia, pronounced mur-sha, in the age of warrior kings.

The largest hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold and silver ever found. Anywhere. Ever.

And it was strange gold. Almost every piece was war gear. Eighty-four sword pommel caps. Seventy-one hilt collars. Helmet fragments. Almost no jewellery, almost nothing a woman would have worn, and, tellingly, not a single blade.

Somebody had taken swords, hundreds of them, and stripped the gold off the handles. Then put the gold in a bag, and put the bag in the ground.

There was a cross in there too. A large processional cross, folded roughly in half to make it fit.

Whoever buried it had no reverence for any of it. It was loot. It was somebody else's defeat, packed away like scrap.

And, exactly like California, they never came back for it.

On the twenty-fifth of November, two thousand and nine, an independent panel called the Treasure Valuation Committee met at the British Museum and put a number on it.

Three million, two hundred and eighty-five thousand pounds.

Under British law, that money is split in half. Half to the finder. Half to the landowner. Two museums, in Birmingham and Stoke-on-Trent, launched a public appeal to raise it and keep the hoard in the region. Schoolchildren sent in coins. They got there.

So a man on disability benefit in a council flat received something in the region of one and a half million pounds. For eighteen years of nothing, followed by five days.

Fred Johnson, the farmer, got the same. Ten years later he told the BBC that he still lived on the farm, still mixed with the same people, and that the money had not changed him. He said people came up to him in town and shook his hand.

But the two men, the friend with the detector and the friend with the field, fell out.

That has been reported repeatedly and never seriously denied, and as far as anyone knows publicly, the rift was never repaired. Neither man has ever fully explained it. I am not going to invent a reason for you, because nobody outside that argument knows what it was.

I will only say this. They had known each other before. One of them had been allowed onto the other's land as a favour. And then, between them, they were handed three and a quarter million pounds, and something in that arrangement broke.

There is a small, cold footnote.

Three years later, in the winter of two thousand and twelve, Fred Johnson ploughed the field again, and more gold came up. Archaeologists had already gone over that ground with equipment used to find buried metal in war zones, and declared it empty. They were wrong. Ninety more pieces came out, including a helmet cheek-piece that fitted a fragment from the original find.

Terry Herbert was not there. He had nothing to do with it. But under the law he was still the finder, so he was still entitled to half.

The field kept paying a man who was no longer speaking to the man who owned it.

Two finds. Two fortunes hauled out of the ground by people who got dirty doing it.

The third one is different. Nothing was buried. Nothing was hidden. The object sat in plain sight, in an ordinary living room in an ordinary suburb, for around eighty years.

And it produced the biggest number in this video... which turned out to be a ghost.

January, two thousand and ten. Pinner, north-west London. A quiet street of semi-detached houses.

A woman called Patricia Newman died there, aged seventy-three, in the house she had shared with her husband. She left no will. Under English law that made her intestate, which meant a court, rather than a family, decided who got everything.

Her only surviving close relative was her sister, Gene Johnson, who was eighty-six years old. Gene's son, Tony Johnson, was fifty-five and a solicitor living on the Isle of Wight, so he handled the paperwork himself. Three months later a court in Winchester signed the estate over to his mother. On paper it came to about six hundred and fifty-eight thousand pounds, and almost all of that was the house.

Then came the part every family knows. Emptying the place. Mahogany furniture, cupboards, a lifetime of ornaments, and somewhere among them, on a shelf, a Chinese vase.

Sixteen inches tall. Blue and yellow. Decorated with fish. It had been in the family since at least the nineteen thirties, and nobody living had any idea how it got there.

They found a leaflet from a local auction house, Bainbridge's, out in Ruislip. A small suburban firm that mostly handled probate clearances and sold things for a few hundred pounds. The leaflet was there because the owner had spent money on a mailshot across north-west London, hoping to bring in exactly this kind of job.

On the evening of the twenty-second of September, a porter lifted the vase onto a shelf reserved for ceramics. A consultant valuer named Luan Grocholski, pronounced gro-hol-ski, who had spent years cataloguing at Sotheby's, walked past it.

He stopped.

The vase was double-walled. An outer shell pierced like lace, and a second vase turning inside it. On the base was a Qianlong reign mark, pronounced chee-en-long, the emperor who ruled China through most of the seventeen hundreds. The enamelling was imperial workshop quality. The kind of object made at Jingdezhen, pronounced jing-duh-jen, for a palace, not a market.

Grocholski went to libraries and looked for anything comparable. There was very little. There is nothing quite like it outside the Palace Museum in Beijing.

They put an estimate on it of eight hundred thousand to one point two million pounds. For a suburban saleroom, that was already the sale of a lifetime.
The eleventh of November, two thousand and ten. Lot eight hundred.

The room was packed. People were standing along the walls. Bidders had flown in. The bidding did not creep. It went through the estimate almost immediately, and then it kept going. Past five million. Past ten. Past twenty. Past thirty. Into a range that no piece of Chinese art had ever reached at auction anywhere in the world.

Forty-three million pounds.

The hammer broke.

With the buyer's premium and the tax on it, the total bill came to fifty-three million, one hundred and five thousand pounds. Around eighty-three million dollars. A world record for any Chinese work of art, set in a beige warehouse next to a car park, by an auctioneer whose usual lots go for under five hundred.

The family had walked in that morning hoping for a million. They walked out, on paper, among the wealthiest people in the country.

On paper.

The winning bid had been made by a man sitting in the front row, bidding on behalf of somebody else. His client's bill was forty-three million, plus a twenty percent buyer's premium on top. Eight point six million pounds in fees.

The money did not arrive.

Not that week. Not that month. Weeks turned into months. The auctioneer and Tony Johnson eventually got on a plane to China to try to find the buyer and collect. They came home with nothing.

Rumours filled the gap. That the buyer was disputing the premium. That the buyer's business had turned. A name has circulated in the press for years, and it has never been confirmed, so I am not going to put it in your head as a fact.

Meanwhile the family was trapped. The conditions of the original sale stopped them simply taking the vase to another auction house. Hold out for forty-three million and you might get nothing. Sell it again and the surprise is gone, everybody has seen it, and no one will ever bid like that twice.

Gene Johnson was eighty-six when the hammer fell. She spent the next two years waiting for money from a sale that had already been announced to the entire world.

In January two thousand and thirteen, it ended quietly. Bonhams brokered a private deal with a different buyer. The price was never disclosed. People with knowledge of the transaction put it somewhere between about twenty and twenty-five million pounds. The record books list it, cautiously, as at least twenty million.

The vase left the country.

The auction house's original bill was never met in full. They received an interim payment, and, by every account, a great deal of grief.

So think about what that number actually was.

Forty-three million pounds existed for about four seconds. As sound in a room, and ink on a board. It broke a gavel, it made headlines in forty countries, and it never became money. What became money was roughly half of it, two years later, in a private deal nobody was allowed to describe.

And yet. A retired solicitor and his elderly mother emptied a dead woman's bungalow and came out of it with something in the region of twenty million pounds, for an ornament that had been sitting on a shelf being dusted for the better part of a century.

Patricia Newman lived with that vase in her front room. She died without a will, aged seventy-three, in a semi-detached house in Pinner, and she never knew.

Three stories. Look at what they have in common.

In every single one, the object outlasted everybody who owned it. Whoever filled those cans in California walked away and died. Whoever buried the Staffordshire gold walked away and died. Whoever carried that vase out of China in the eighteen hundreds put it on a shelf, and within two generations it was just an ornament nobody looked at.

None of these people were lucky, exactly. They were the ones who bothered to look.

She bent down for a rusty can that a hundred other people would have kicked. He kept swinging a two pound fifty detector through an empty field after eighteen years of finding nothing. He picked up a leaflet from a suburban auction house instead of calling a clearance firm to take the lot away for fifty quid.

That is the whole difference. Not luck. Attention.

So here is my question for you, and I actually want to read the answers.

Which of the three would you rather be? The couple who got ten million dollars and can never tell a single person? The man who got one and a half million and lost the friend who let him onto the land? Or the family who set a world record, and then waited two years to find out if it was real?

Tell me down below. I read them.

And if you want more of these, there are plenty. The ground is full of them.

youtube.title: 3 Finds. 70 Million Dollars. All Nearly Thrown Out.
title_alternatives: Why Was This GBP43,000,000 Vase Never Paid For?
He Kicked Past It For Years. Then He Looked Down.
youtube.description_intro: A rusty can on a footpath. A ploughed field in Staffordshire. A vase on a shelf in a suburban living room. Three ordinary people found roughly seventy million dollars in objects that almost everybody else had already walked past - and every one of them paid a price for it that nobody mentions. One of the three record numbers in this video was never actually paid at all.
chapters: The gavel that broke, and a can in the mud
Ten million dollars nobody can claim
Five days that ended a friendship
